title: PBS station fears losing 50TB of data after being ghosted by cloud storage provider
gist: St. Louis PBS affiliate Nine PBS sued Iron Mountain Data Centers on July 28, 2026 in Denver District Court to recover 50TB and 11,000+ files of 70-year-old archival broadcast material after its cloud storage vendor Open Source Storage went delinquent and stopped responding. The case exposes the colocation stack's liability gap: Iron Mountain rents space and says it has no access to customer-owned servers, so a bankrupt intermediary can strand an end customer's data even when a court confirms the customer owns it.

insights.claim: Iron Mountain refused to release Nine PBS's data because its contract is only with intermediary Open Source Storage and because OSS owns the physical servers housing the data, illustrating that colocation providers owe no duty to their customers' customers.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Enterprises buying cloud from resellers have no privity with the underlying data center and therefore no direct recovery path when the reseller fails.
insights.locator: However, Iron Mountain refused to give Nine PBS the data

insights.claim: Iron Mountain states it provides only physical infrastructure — building, network connectivity, power and environmental controls — and has no access to data on customer-owned hardware racked in its facilities.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: The colo business model deliberately excludes data custody, which caps liability but also caps the operational value it can offer in a vendor-failure scenario.
insights.quote: Our customers rent space for their servers and other hardware. These are the client's assets. We don't have access to the data on the hardware/servers because they belong to our customers

insights.claim: Iron Mountain argues that granting unauthorized access to third-party hardware without a court order would violate basic data privacy protocols, breach its contract with OSS, and potentially expose confidential data belonging to other OSS clients.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant hardware makes selective data release legally impossible without judicial cover, guaranteeing months of delay in any vendor-collapse recovery.
insights.quote: potentially [exposing] confidential data belonging to other clients of OSS
insights.locator: Iron Mountain said the company would violate basic data privacy protocols

insights.claim: Iron Mountain publicly maintains it acted appropriately and responsibly at every step, was transparent with Nine PBS that it does not have access to their data, and honored its contractual commitments to OSS.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Iron Mountain is positioning contractual fidelity to its direct counterparty as the defense — relevant to how colo reputational risk actually resolves.
insights.quote: Iron Mountain has acted appropriately and responsibly at every step to safeguard customer data and honor our contractual commitments to OSS.
insights.locator: When reached for comment, an Iron Mountain spokesperson

themes.theme: How a storage vendor silently evaporated

insights.claim: Open Source Storage, formed in 2021, went unresponsive to Nine PBS's February contract-renewal inquiries, ceased operations, and holds delinquent status with the Colorado Secretary of State's business database.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: State business-registry status is a cheap, underused early-warning signal for vendor viability in procurement due diligence.
insights.locator: The channel says it then learned that OSS had delinquency status

insights.claim: Nine PBS's contract nominally gave it 30 days to retrieve data at contract end, but the station abruptly lost access the moment the contract expired on March 6 — showing that contractual egress windows are worthless once a vendor stops operating.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Egress rights must be exercised before renewal risk materializes; post-termination retrieval clauses provide no protection against insolvency.
insights.locator: The station claims its contract gave it 30 days to retrieve data

insights.claim: James Tramel, described as managing partner of the group that acquired OSS's assets, told Nine PBS that Iron Mountain held its data, then stopped responding after saying by phone that he had been defrauded into buying OSS and was no longer affiliated with the company.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Distressed asset acquirers can walk away, leaving no solvent party with both authority and incentive to release stranded customer data.
insights.locator: James Tramel, who the complaint describes as a managing partner

insights.claim: Nine PBS won a default judgment against OSS in St. Louis Circuit Court establishing its immediate right to possess the data and ordering OSS to return it or facilitate transfer to a new vendor, yet the judgment did not produce the data because OSS no longer exists to comply.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Legal ownership of data confers nothing operationally when the party holding physical control is a non-party to the judgment.
insights.quote: immediate right to possess the data
insights.locator: Nine PBS eventually won a default judgment against the company

insights.claim: Nine PBS filed suit against Iron Mountain Data Centers on July 28, 2026 in Denver District Court seeking access to 50TB of TV shows, videos and other data dating back 70 years, including over 11,000 files most of which the complaint calls unique and irreplaceable.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Sets a live precedent for whether an end customer can compel a colo landlord to surrender a defunct tenant's hardware.
insights.locator: St. Louis affiliate Nine PBS filed a lawsuit against Iron Mountain

insights.claim: A judge blocked Iron Mountain from deleting or modifying the disputed data in July 2026, and in a subsequent Wednesday hearing ruled that Iron Mountain must hand over any physical devices holding the data.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Courts are willing to order physical device transfer from colo operators — a meaningful expansion of exposure for infrastructure landlords.
insights.locator: Last month, a judge blocked Iron Mountain from deleting

insights.claim: The court required Nine PBS to find a third party such as a former OSS worker to retrieve the data within 30 days without sharing or corrupting data belonging to other OSS clients, and Nine PBS is already in contact with a willing former OSS employee.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Recovery hinges on tacit knowledge held by ex-employees of a dead company — an unpriced dependency in any vendor-failure plan.
insights.locator: The judge also said that Nine PBS must find a third party

insights.claim: If complications such as data encryption arise, another hearing will be scheduled, and Nine PBS and Iron Mountain must provide status updates by September 14, 2026.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Encryption keys held only by the defunct vendor would render physical possession of the drives worthless — the key unresolved risk in the case.
insights.locator: If complications arise, such as from the data being encrypted

insights.claim: Nine PBS did not answer whether it held any backups of the 50TB archive or what it would do to prevent a recurrence, leaving open whether the station relied on a single unreplicated vendor for irreplaceable material.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Single-vendor archives without independent copies are a live operational risk category for media, cultural and public-sector institutions.
insights.quote: Ars asked Nine PBS if it had any backups of the data and what the station would do to prevent this from happening again, but we didn't receive answers as of publication time.
insights.locator: Ars asked Nine PBS if it had any backups

insights.claim: The stranded archive includes Nine PBS's coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic, East St. Louis' history and The Great Flood of 1993, giving the dispute regional cultural-heritage stakes beyond commercial data loss.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Public-interest content raises the odds of favorable judicial treatment and of policy attention to archival custody rules.
insights.locator: The data in question includes the station's coverage

insights.claim: Nine PBS offered on March 13 to pay any reasonable costs associated with accessing its data, and Iron Mountain still declined, showing the blocker was contractual and legal rather than economic.
insights.speaker: Scharon Harding
insights.so_what: Money cannot unlock a data-custody deadlock structured around contractual privity — only litigation or pre-negotiated escrow terms can.
